claim: The activity of type I MADS-box TFs is associated with the timing of endosperm cellularization in Arabidopsis thaliana and other species.

source: Nevertheless, the observation that a considerable proportion of genes show an endosperm expression pattern that mimics PHE1 expression (Figure 1b–c), and also show upregulation upon PHE1 overexpression (Figure 1d–e), suggests that PHE1 acts as a transcriptional activator, and validates the binding sites obtained through ChIP-seq.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis revealed enriched GO-terms associated with brassinosteroid signaling pathways, seed growth and development, and metabolic pathways.
source: To explore the functional role of PHE1 targets, we performed a Gene Ontology (GO) analysis (Figure 2a). This revealed several different enriched GO-terms associated with brassinosteroid signaling pathways, seed growth and development, and metabolic pathways including triglyceride biosynthesis and carbohydrate transport.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GO analysis and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: An enrichment of a GO-term associated with positive regulation of transcription was found among PHE1 targets.
source: Furthermore, we found an enrichment of a GO-term associated with the positive regulation of transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GO analysis.

claim: Many PHE1 targets are themselves transcriptional regulators.
source: Indeed, many PHE1 targets are themselves transcriptional regulators (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the analysis of PHE1 targets and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Type I MADS-box family genes are strongly over-represented among PHE1 targets.
source: More specifically, we detected that other type I MADS-box family genes are strongly over-represented among PHE1 targets (Figure 2b), pointing to a high degree of cross-regulation among members of this family.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the analysis of PHE1 targets and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There is a high degree of cross-regulation among type I MADS-box family members.
source: More specifically, we detected that other type I MADS-box family genes are strongly over-represented among PHE1 targets (Figure 2b), pointing to a high degree of cross-regulation among members of this family.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed over-representation of type I MADS-box genes among PHE1 targets.

claim: Several PHE1 targets, such as AGL62, YUC10, IKU2, MINI3, and ZHOUPI, are known regulators of seed development.
source: In addition, several PHE1 targets , such as AGL62, YUC10, IKU2, MINI3, and ZHOUPI, are known regulators of seed development (Table 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the identification of these genes as PHE1 targets and established knowledge about their functions.

claim: AGL62, YUC10, IKU2, MINI3, and ZHOUPI have been previously described to influence the proliferation, cellularization, and breakdown of the endosperm.
source: These genes have been previously described to influence the proliferation, cellularization, and breakdown of the endosperm (Table 3), revealing an important role for PHE1 in regulating the development of this structure.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references in Table 3.

claim: PHE1 has an important role in regulating endosperm development.
source: These genes have been previously described to influence the proliferation, cellularization, and breakdown of the endosperm (Table 3), revealing an important role for PHE1 in regulating the development of this structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that PHE1 targets known regulators of endosperm development.

claim: PHE1 uses two distinct DNA-binding motifs: motif A and motif B.
source: To investigate the DNA-binding properties of PHE1, we screened PHE1 binding sites for enriched sequence motifs, using HOMER's de novo motif analysis tool. This analysis revealed that PHE1 uses two distinct DNA-binding motifs: motif A was present in about 53% of PHE1 binding sites, and motif B could also be found in 43% of those sites (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Motif A is present in about 53% of PHE1 binding sites.
source: To investigate the DNA-binding properties of PHE1, we screened PHE1 binding sites for enriched sequence motifs, using HOMER's de novo motif analysis tool. This analysis revealed that PHE1 uses two distinct DNA-binding motifs: motif A was present in about 53% of PHE1 binding sites, and motif B could also be found in 43% of those sites (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Motif B is present in about 43% of PHE1 binding sites.
source: To investigate the DNA-binding properties of PHE1, we screened PHE1 binding sites for enriched sequence motifs, using HOMER's de novo motif analysis tool. This analysis revealed that PHE1 uses two distinct DNA-binding motifs: motif A was present in about 53% of PHE1 binding sites, and motif B could also be found in 43% of those sites (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: 68% of all PHE1 binding sites are associated with at least one of the two motifs.
source: In total, 68% of all of PHE1 binding sites are associated with at least one of these motifs, and the majority of these show co-occurrence of Motif A and B (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The majority of PHE1 binding sites with motifs show co-occurrence of Motif A and B.
source: In total, 68% of all of PHE1 binding sites are associated with at least one of these motifs, and the majority of these show co-occurrence of Motif A and B (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The highest density of PHE1 DNA-binding motifs is detected at the center of PHE1 binding sites.
source: In addition, and as observed for type II MADS-box TFs (Aerts et al., 2018), the highest density of these motifs is detected at the center of PHE1 binding sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: PHE1 DNA-binding motifs closely resemble CArG-boxes, the signature motif of binding sites for type II MADS-box TFs.
source: PHE1 DNA-binding motifs closely resemble CArG-boxes, the signature motif of binding sites for type II MADS-box TFs (de Folter and Angenent, 2006) (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis and comparison to known motifs, shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Motif B is similar to the SEP3 DNA-binding motif and shows the characteristics of a bona fide CArG-box.
source: This is particularly visible in the case of Motif B, which is similar to the SEP3 DNA-binding motif, and shows the characteristics of a bona fide CArG-box -– CC(A/T)6GG (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis and comparison to known motifs, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Motif A shows similarity to the SVP CArG-box but lacks the terminal G nucleotides, resembling a partially degenerated CArG-box.
source: Motif A, on the other hand, shows similarity to the SVP CArG-box, but lacks the terminal G nucleotides, thus resembling a partially degenerated CArG-box (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis and comparison to known motifs, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The DNA-binding properties of type I and type II TFs might be conserved.
source: Nevertheless, the detected similarity between PHE1 DNA-binding motifs and previously characterized CArG-boxes suggests that the DNA-binding properties of type I and type II TFs might be conserved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed similarity between PHE1 motifs and CArG-boxes.

claim: PHE1 binding sites significantly overlap with TEs, preferentially with those of the RC/Helitron superfamily.
source: Strikingly, we observed that PHE1 binding sites significantly overlap with TEs, preferentially with those of the RC/Helitron superfamily (29% in PHE1 binding sites, versus 9% in random binding sites) (Figure 3b), and in particular with some RC/Helitron subfamilies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TE overlap analysis and shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 29% of PHE1 binding sites overlap with RC/Helitron TEs, versus 9% in random binding sites.
source: Strikingly, we observed that PHE1 binding sites significantly overlap with TEs, preferentially with those of the RC/Helitron superfamily (29% in PHE1 binding sites, versus 9% in random binding sites) (Figure 3b), and in particular with some RC/Helitron subfamilies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TE overlap analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: RC/Helitrons contain significantly higher PHE1 DNA-binding motif densities when compared to other TE superfamilies.
source: We thus addressed the question of whether RC/Helitrons contain sequence properties that promote PHE1 binding. Indeed, a screen of genomic regions for the presence of PHE1 DNA-binding motifs, revealed significantly higher motif densities within all RC/Helitrons, when compared to other TE superfamilies (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif density analysis and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Most RC/Helitron sequences associated with PHE1 DNA-binding motifs share sequence homology.
source: We found that most RC/Helitron sequences associated with PHE1 DNA-binding motifs share sequence homology, and that the majority of them could be grouped into one large cluster on the basis of sequence identity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sequence homology analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: A single ancestral RC/Helitron probably acquired a perfect or nearly perfect PHE1 DNA-binding motif.
source: Although the presence of additional smaller clusters points to a few instances of independent gains of PHE1 DNA-binding motifs through de novo mutation or sequence capture, the grouping of most sequences within one cluster suggests that a single ancestral RC/Helitron probably acquired a perfect or nearly perfect motif.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed clustering of RC/Helitron sequences.

claim: Perfect or nearly perfect PHE1 DNA-binding motifs are present within the consensus sequences of several RC/Helitron families.
source: Moreover, we could detect the presence of perfect or nearly perfect PHE1 DNA-binding motifs within the consensus sequences of several RC/Helitron families (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the radiation of RC/Helitrons occurred after the acquisition of the binding motif.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis of consensus sequences and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The radiation of RC/Helitrons occurred after the acquisition of the PHE1 binding motif.
source: Moreover, we could detect the presence of perfect or nearly perfect PHE1 DNA-binding motifs within the consensus sequences of several RC/Helitron families (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the radiation of RC/Helitrons occurred after the acquisition of the binding motif.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of motifs in consensus sequences.

claim: Genes flanked by RC/Helitrons carrying bound PHE1 DNA-binding motifs are expressed to a greater level in the endosperm than in other seed tissues.
source: In line with this, we detected that genes that are flanked by RC/Helitrons carrying bound PHE1 DNA-binding motifs were expressed to a greater level in the endosperm than in other seed tissues, and were expressed at levels similar to those of PHE1 targets without flanking RC/Helitrons (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by gene expression analysis and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: For a subset of genes, TEs can be effectively used as sites for PHE1 binding, triggering endosperm-specific expression of nearby genes.
source: This shows that for a subset of genes, TEs can be effectively used as sites for PHE1 binding, thus triggering the endosperm-specific expression of nearby genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression patterns of genes flanked by RC/Helitrons with PHE1 binding motifs.

claim: 9% of all maternally expressed genes (MEGs) are targeted by PHE1.
source: We detected a significant enrichment of imprinted genes among the PHE1 target genes, with 9% of all maternally expressed genes (MEGs) and 27% of all paternally expressed genes (PEGs) being targeted (Figure 4a, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the analysis of PHE1 targets and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: 27% of all paternally expressed genes (PEGs) are targeted by PHE1.
source: We detected a significant enrichment of imprinted genes among the PHE1 target genes, with 9% of all maternally expressed genes (MEGs) and 27% of all paternally expressed genes (PEGs) being targeted (Figure 4a, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the analysis of PHE1 targets and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of imprinted genes among PHE1 target genes.
source: We detected a significant enrichment of imprinted genes among the PHE1 target genes, with 9% of all maternally expressed genes (MEGs) and 27% of all paternally expressed genes (PEGs) being targeted (Figure 4a, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the analysis of PHE1 targets and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Two distinct clusters of PHE1 binding sites were identified based on H3K27me3 levels.
source: We surveyed levels of endosperm H3K27me3 within PHE1-binding sites and identified two distinct clusters (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Cluster 1 is characterized by an accumulation of H3K27me3 in regions flanking the center of the binding site, with the center itself devoid of this mark.
source: Cluster 1 was characterized by an accumulation of H3K27me3 in regions flanking the center of the binding site, whereas the center itself was devoid of this mark.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data.

claim: Binding of PHE1 at cluster 1 sites occurs in an H3K27me3-depleted island.
source: This pattern of distribution was maintained when taking into consideration the strand location of the gene associated with the binding site, revealing that binding of PHE1 at these sites occurs in an H3K27me3-depleted island (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cluster 2 contains binding sites that are largely devoid of H3K27me3.
source: Cluster 2, on the other hand, contained binding sites that are largely devoid of H3K27me3.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data.

claim: The distribution of H3K27me3 in cluster 1 is mostly attributed to deposition on maternal alleles, whereas paternal alleles are devoid of this mark.
source: The distribution of H3K27me3 in cluster 1 was mostly attributed to the deposition of H3K27me3 on the maternal alleles, whereas the paternal alleles were devoid of this mark (Figure 4c) — a pattern usually associated with PEGs (Moreno-Romero et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by parental-specific H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Genes associated with cluster 1 binding sites have more paternally biased expression in the endosperm than genes associated with cluster 2.
source: Consistently, genes that are associated with cluster 1 binding sites had more paternally biased expression in the endosperm when compared to genes associated with cluster 2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by gene expression data and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: More PEGs and putative PEGs are associated with cluster 1 than cluster 2.
source: This is reflected by the association of more PEGs and putative PEGs with cluster 1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the analysis of imprinted genes and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: PHE1-binding sites associated with MEGs have significantly higher CG methylation levels in paternal alleles than in maternal alleles.
source: We also identified parental-specific differences in DNA methylation, specifically in the CG context: PHE1-binding sites that were associated with MEGs had significantly higher methylation levels in paternal alleles than in maternal alleles (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by DNA methylation data and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Differential parental deposition of epigenetic marks in parental alleles of PHE1 binding sites can result in differential accessibility of each allele.
source: We hypothesized that the differential parental deposition of epigenetic marks in parental alleles of PHE1 binding sites can result in the differential accessibility of each allele.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the observed data.

claim: Differential accessibility of parental alleles might impact the binding of PHE1 and transcription in a parent-of-origin-specific manner.
source: We hypothesized that the differential parental deposition of epigenetic marks in parental alleles of PHE1 binding sites can result in the differential accessibility of each allele. This might impact the binding of PHE1, and therefore also impact transcription in a parent-of-origin-specific manner.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the observed data.

claim: Binding of PHE1 is biallelic in non-imprinted targets.
source: Although binding of PHE1 was biallelic in non-imprinted targets (Figure 4e), only maternal binding was detected in the tested MEG targets (Figure 4e), supporting the idea that CG hypermethylation of paternal alleles prevents their binding by PHE1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by parental-specific PHE1 ChIP and Sanger sequencing, shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Only maternal binding of PHE1 was detected in tested MEG targets.
source: Although binding of PHE1 was biallelic in non-imprinted targets (Figure 4e), only maternal binding was detected in the tested MEG targets (Figure 4e), supporting the idea that CG hypermethylation of paternal alleles prevents their binding by PHE1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by parental-specific PHE1 ChIP and Sanger sequencing, shown in Figure 4e.

claim: CG hypermethylation of paternal alleles prevents their binding by PHE1.
source: Although binding of PHE1 was biallelic in non-imprinted targets (Figure 4e), only maternal binding was detected in the tested MEG targets (Figure 4e), supporting the idea that CG hypermethylation of paternal alleles prevents their binding by PHE1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed maternal-only binding in MEG targets and the presence of CG hypermethylation on paternal alleles.

claim: Biallelic binding of PHE1 was observed in PEG targets.
source: Interestingly, we observed biallelic binding in PEG targets (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by parental-specific PHE1 ChIP and Sanger sequencing, shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The absence of H3K27me3 within the binding site centers of PEGs seems to be permissive for maternal PHE1 binding.
source: Even though the maternal PHE1 binding sites in PEGs were flanked by H3K27me3 (Figure 4b–c), correlating with the transcriptional repression of maternal alleles, the absence of this mark within the binding site centers seems to be permissive for maternal PHE1 binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed biallelic binding in PEG targets despite H3K27me3 flanking the binding sites.

claim: PEGs are often flanked by RC/Helitrons.
source: Previous studies have shown that PEGs are often flanked by RC/Helitrons (Hatorangan et al., 2016; Pignatta et al., 2014; Wolff et al., 2011), a phenomenon that has been suggested to lead to the parental asymmetry of epigenetic marks in these genes (Moreno-Romero et al., 2016; Pignatta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: RC/Helitrons flanking PEGs have been suggested to lead to parental asymmetry of epigenetic marks in these genes.
source: Previous studies have shown that PEGs are often flanked by RC/Helitrons (Hatorangan et al., 2016; Pignatta et al., 2014; Wolff et al., 2011), a phenomenon that has been suggested to lead to the parental asymmetry of epigenetic marks in these genes (Moreno-Romero et al., 2016; Pignatta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: PHE1 DNA-binding motifs are contained within RC/Helitrons significantly more frequently in PEGs than in non-imprinted genes.
source: Consistent with our finding that PHE1 binding sites overlapped with RC/Helitrons (Figure 3b), we found that PHE1 DNA-binding motifs were contained within these TEs significantly more frequently in PEGs than in non-imprinted genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif and TE overlap analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Homologous RC/Helitrons containing PHE1 binding motifs are present in the promoter regions of several PHE1-targeted PEG orthologs.
source: Furthermore, we detected the presence of homologous RC/Helitrons containing PHE1 binding motifs in the promoter regions of several PHE1-targeted PEG orthologs (Figure 5a–e, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating ancestral insertion events.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by phylogenetic analysis and sequence alignment, shown in Figure 5a-e and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of RC/Helitrons with PHE1 binding motifs indicates ancestral insertion events.
source: Furthermore, we detected the presence of homologous RC/Helitrons containing PHE1 binding motifs in the promoter regions of several PHE1-targeted PEG orthologs (Figure 5a–e, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating ancestral insertion events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of homologous RC/Helitrons in orthologous genes.

claim: The presence of RC/Helitrons with PHE1 binding motifs correlates with paternally biased expression of the associated orthologs.
source: The presence of these RC/Helitrons correlated with paternally biased expression of the associated orthologs, providing further support to the hypothesis that these TEs contribute to the gain of imprinting, especially of PEGs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by phylogenetic analysis and gene expression data.

claim: RC/Helitrons contribute to the gain of imprinting, especially of PEGs.
source: The presence of these RC/Helitrons correlated with paternally biased expression of the associated orthologs, providing further support to the hypothesis that these TEs contribute to the gain of imprinting, especially of PEGs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between RC/Helitron presence and paternally biased expression.

claim: ADM, SUVH7, PEG2, and NRPD1a are PEGs targeted by PHE1.
source: Among the PEGs that were targeted by PHE1 were ADM, SUVH7, PEG2, and NRPD1a (Table 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Mutants in ADM, SUVH7, PEG2, and NRPD1a suppress the abortion of 3x seeds generated by paternal excess interploidy crosses.
source: Mutants in all four PEGs suppress the abortion of 3x seeds generated by paternal excess interploidy crosses (Martinez et al., 2018; Satyaki and Gehring, 2019; Wolff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Between 40% and 50% of highly upregulated genes in 3x seeds are targeted by PHE1.
source: Furthermore, we found that between 40% and 50% of highly upregulated genes in 3x seeds are targeted by PHE1 (Figure 6a), suggesting that this TF might play a central role in mediating the strong gene deregulation observed in these seeds.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by transcriptomics data and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: PHE1 might play a central role in mediating the strong gene deregulation observed in 3x seeds.
source: Furthermore, we found that between 40% and 50% of highly upregulated genes in 3x seeds are targeted by PHE1 (Figure 6a), suggesting that this TF might play a central role in mediating the strong gene deregulation observed in these seeds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that a large proportion of upregulated genes in 3x seeds are PHE1 targets.

claim: Removal of PHE1 in paternal excess 3x seeds is expected to suppress their inviability.
source: If this is true, removal of PHE1 in paternal excess 3x seeds is expected to suppress their inviability.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the observed role of PHE1 in gene deregulation.

claim: phe1 phe2 osd1 pollen strongly suppresses 3x seed inviability.
source: Indeed, although wt and phe2 maternal plants pollinated with osd1 pollen form 3x seeds that abort at high frequency (Kradolfer et al., 2013), phe1 phe2 osd1 pollen strongly suppresses 3x seed inviability (Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by seed viability assays and shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: 3x phe1 phe2 seeds show increased germination.
source: This is also reflected by the increased germination of 3x phe1 phe2 seeds (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b), and this phenotype could be reverted by introducing the PHE1::PHE1–GFP transgene paternally (Figure 6b–c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by seed germination assays and shown in Figure 6c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The increased germination phenotype of 3x phe1 phe2 seeds can be reverted by introducing the PHE1::PHE1–GFP transgene paternally.
source: This is also reflected by the increased germination of 3x phe1 phe2 seeds (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b), and this phenotype could be reverted by introducing the PHE1::PHE1–GFP transgene paternally (Figure 6b–c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by seed germination assays and shown in Figure 6b-c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: 3x seed rescue is mostly mediated by phe1.
source: Notably, 3x seed rescue was mostly mediated by phe1, as the presence of a wt PHE2 allele in 3x seeds (wt x phe1 phe2 osd1) led to rescue levels that were comparable to those seen when no wt PHE2 allele was present (phe2 x phe1 phe2 osd1) (Figure 6b–c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by seed viability and germination assays, shown in Figure 6b-c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: phe1-mediated 3x seed rescue is accompanied by reestablishment of endosperm cellularization.
source: Importantly, phe1-mediated 3x seed rescue was accompanied by reestablishment of endosperm cellularization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by endosperm cellularization assays and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: Loss of FIS-PRC2 function causes a phenotype similar to that of paternal excess 3x seeds.
source: Loss of FIS-PRC2 function causes a phenotype similar to that of paternal excess 3x seeds, correlating with largely overlapping sets of deregulated genes, notably PEGs (Erilova et al., 2009; Tiwari et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: FIS-PRC2 is a major regulator of PEGs in the Arabidopsis endosperm.
source: As FIS-PRC2 is a major regulator of PEGs in the Arabidopsis endosperm (Moreno-Romero et al., 2016), we addressed the question of whether imprinting is disrupted in 3x seeds.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Imprinting is not disrupted in 3x seeds.
source: To assess this, we analyzed the parental expression ratio of imprinted genes in the endosperm of 2x and 3x seeds. Surprisingly, imprinting was not disrupted in 3x seeds (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by parental-specific gene expression data and shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Similar H3K27me3 levels are detected on the maternal alleles of PEGs in 2x and 3x seeds.
source: To confirm that maintenance of imprinting in 3x seeds is explained by maintenance of the underlying epigenetic marks, we generated parental-specific H3K27me3 profiles of 2x and 3x seed endosperm (Table 4). Consistent with the observed maintenance of imprinting, we detected similar H3K27me3 levels on the maternal alleles of PEGs in 2x and 3x seeds (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by parental-specific H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data and shown in Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The major upregulation of PEG expression in 3x seeds is due to increased transcription of the active allele, probably mediated by PHE1 and other MADS-box TFs, with maintenance of the imprinting status.
source: Collectively, these data show that the major upregulation of PEG expression in 3x seeds is due to increased transcription of the active allele, probably mediated by PHE1 and other MADS-box TFs, with maintenance of the imprinting status.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed maintenance of imprinting and H3K27me3 levels in 3x seeds.

claim: PHE1 is expressed during the early stages of seed development, immediately after fertilization, and until the onset of endosperm cellularization.
source: PHE1 is expressed during the early stages of seed development, immediately after fertilization, and until the onset of endosperm cellularization.
evidence: This is a statement about the expression pattern of PHE1.

claim: The initial stages of endosperm development are characterised by rapid proliferation accompanied by import of resources to this tissue.
source: The initial stages of endosperm development are characterised by a rapid proliferation that is accompanied by import of resources to this tissue (Hill et al., 2003; Mansfield and Briarty, 1990; Morley-Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Upon cellularization, resources are hypothesized to be transferred to the embryo, correlating with rapid growth and accumulation of storage products in this structure.
source: Upon cellularization, these resources are hypothesized to be transferred to the embryo, correlating with rapid growth and the accumulation of storage products in this structure (Baud et al., 2008; Hehenberger et al., 2012; Hill et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Genes required for endosperm proliferation and growth, such as YUC10, IKU2, and MINI3, are under transcriptional control of PHE1.
source: Remarkably, we found that genes that are required for endosperm proliferation and growth, such as YUC10 (Figueiredo et al., 2015), IKU2 (Garcia et al., 2003; Luo et al., 2005), and MINI3 (Luo et al., 2005) are under transcriptional control of PHE1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Proliferation of the endosperm becomes dependent on the presence of the paternal genome because PHE1 is imprinted and paternally expressed.
source: As PHE1 is imprinted and paternally expressed (Köhler et al., 2005), proliferation of the endosperm becomes dependent on the presence of the paternal genome, which allows the fertilization event to be coupled with the onset of endosperm growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the imprinted and paternally expressed nature of PHE1 and its role in regulating endosperm proliferation genes.

claim: PHE1 might have an important role in resource accumulation in preparation for cellularization.
source: Besides being relevant for endosperm proliferation, PHE1 might also have an important role in resource accumulation in preparation for cellularization, because genes that are related to metabolic processes, such as carbohydrate transport and triglyceride biosynthesis, were found to be enriched among PHE1 targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed enrichment of metabolic process genes among PHE1 targets.

claim: Type I MADS-box TFs might have a central role in establishing essential transcriptional networks that facilitate endosperm development.
source: The control of both endosperm proliferation and resource accumulation by PHE1 suggests that type I MADS-box TFs might have a central role in establishing essential transcriptional networks that facilitate endosperm development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed roles of PHE1 in endosperm development.

claim: Many other type I MADS-box TFs are expressed in the endosperm.
source: Besides PHE1, many other type I MADS-box TFs are expressed in the endosperm (Bemer et al., 2010), and probably act as heterodimers (de Folter et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Type I MADS-box TFs probably act as heterodimers.
source: Besides PHE1, many other type I MADS-box TFs are expressed in the endosperm (Bemer et al., 2010), and probably act as heterodimers (de Folter et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Different type I MADS-box heterodimers could control distinct sets of genes during endosperm development.
source: Similarly to the function of type II MADS-box TFs in the determination of flower morphology (Chen et al., 2018; Smaczniak et al., 2017; Theissen and Saedler, 2001), different type I MADS-box heterodimers could be able to control distinct sets of genes during endosperm development.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known function of type II MADS-box TFs.

claim: Different stages of endosperm development could be characterized by the activity of different heterodimers.
source: Furthermore, different stages of endosperm development could be characterized by the activity of different heterodimers.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential role of type I MADS-box TFs.

claim: Normal endosperm development is associated with decreased expression of a subset of type I MADS-box genes, including PHE, preceding the onset of cellularization.
source: Normal endosperm development is associated with decreased expression of a subset of type I MADS-box genes, including PHE, preceding the onset of cellularization (Erilova et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2012; Schatlowski and Köhler, 2012; Stoute et al., 2012; Tiwari et al., 2010; Walia et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Type I MADS-box TFs have been suggested to be negative regulators of endosperm cellularization.
source: This has led to the suggestion that these TFs are negative regulators of endosperm cellularization, although the molecular mechanism behind these observations has remained elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about a previous hypothesis in the field.

claim: PHE1 controls the expression of a large fraction of deregulated genes in interploidy hybridization seeds.
source: Our observation that PHE1 controls the expression of a large fraction of deregulated genes in interploidy hybridization seeds, in which cellularization is disturbed, provides an explanation for why the onset of endosperm cellularization is correlated with the expression of PHE1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by transcriptomics data.

claim: PHE1 expression is increased in the endosperm of paternal excess crosses.
source: Because PHE1 expression is increased in the endosperm of paternal excess crosses, the expression of PHE targets is probably similarly affected.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and the observed role of PHE1.

claim: Increased expression of YUC10 leads to prolonged auxin biosynthesis and overaccumulation of this hormone in the endosperm, preventing the onset of cellularization.
source: In the specific case of the target gene YUC10, this leads to prolonged auxin biosynthesis and to the overaccumulation of this hormone in the endosperm, which has been previously shown to prevent the onset of cellularization (Batista et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Successful and adequately timed endosperm cellularization requires a specific pattern of expression of type I MADS-box genes and a balanced stoichiometry between members of different MADS-box protein complexes.
source: Therefore, successful and adequately timed endosperm cellularization probably requires a specific pattern of expression of type I MADS-box genes, as well as a balanced stoichiometry between members of different MADS-box protein complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed role of PHE1 and type I MADS-box TFs in endosperm cellularization.

claim: Interploidy and interspecies hybridizations can easily change the expression and stoichiometry of MADS-box TFs.
source: Interploidy and interspecies hybridizations can easily change the expression and stoichiometry of MADS-box TFs, for example by having distinct numbers of gene copies, or through differences in gene regulation between parents, such as variations in imprinting patterns (Dilkes and Comai, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: Type I MADS-box TFs can function as sensors of parental compatibility in the endosperm.
source: Therefore, it is possible that type I MADS-box TFs can function as sensors of parental compatibility in the endosperm: i) these TFs show expression differences upon interploidy/interspecies hybridization (Erilova et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2012; Schatlowski and Köhler, 2012; Stoute et al., 2012; Tiwari et al., 2010; Walia et al., 2009); and ii) as exemplified here by PHE1, they are able to engage pathways that enforce seed abortion when compatibility between parents is not present.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed roles of type I MADS-box TFs.

claim: Many imprinted genes are targets of PHE1.
source: Here, we report that many imprinted genes are targets of PHE1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Binding of PHE1 to maternal and paternal alleles of some imprinted genes is conditioned by the epigenetic status of the alleles.
source: Interestingly, we observed that binding of PHE1 to maternal and paternal alleles of some of these genes is conditioned by the epigenetic status of the alleles.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by parental-specific PHE1 ChIP data.

claim: DNA methylation near the TSS region has a negative effect on gene expression.
source: The accumulation of DNA methylation near the TSS region has been reported to have a negative effect on gene expression (Niederhuth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: DNA methylation impairs the binding of a wide range of plant TFs.
source: In line with this, DNA methylation was shown to impair the binding of a wide range of plant TFs (O'Malley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: CG methylation restricts the binding of PHE1 to the paternal alleles of tested MEGs.
source: Our observation that CG methylation restricts the binding of PHE1 to the paternal alleles of the tested MEGs is similar to observations made on the mammalian Peg3 gene, where the TF YY1 shows methylation-dependent binding (Kim, 2003).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by parental-specific PHE1 ChIP data.

claim: In plants, as in animals, parental asymmetries of DNA methylation at cis-regulatory regions can lead to parent-of-origin-specific expression patterns.
source: Thus, our data reveal that in plants, as in animals, parental asymmetries of DNA methylation at cis-regulatory regions can lead to parent-of-origin-specific expression patterns (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed parental-specific binding of PHE1 and comparison to mammalian systems.

claim: The H3K27me3-depleted island in maternal alleles of PEGs could be important for PHE1-mediated recruitment of PRC2 complexes in the endosperm.
source: We speculate that this island could be important for PHE1-mediated recruitment of PRC2 complexes in the endosperm and, consequently, for the maintenance of H3K27me3 levels during its proliferation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed H3K27me3 distribution and biallelic PHE1 binding in PEGs.

claim: Plant PRC2 can be recruited by different families of TFs.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the findings that plant PRC2 can be recruited by different families of TFs (Xiao et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018), and that the presence of cis-regulatory features such as Polycomb response elements is essential for maintenance of H3K27me3 upon cell division (Coleman and Struhl, 2017; Laprell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: The presence of cis-regulatory features such as Polycomb response elements is essential for maintenance of H3K27me3 upon cell division.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the findings that plant PRC2 can be recruited by different families of TFs (Xiao et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018), and that the presence of cis-regulatory features such as Polycomb response elements is essential for maintenance of H3K27me3 upon cell division (Coleman and Struhl, 2017; Laprell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Recruitment of H3K27me3 at imprinted loci takes place in the central cell and is faithfully inherited in the endosperm after fertilization.
source: The recruitment of this epigenetic mark at imprinted loci takes place in the central cell, and is faithfully inherited in the endosperm after fertilization (Gehring, 2013; Rodrigues and Zilberman, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: MADS-box DNA-binding motifs can be shared between different MADS-box TFs.
source: Given that MADS-box DNA-binding motifs can be shared between different MADS-box TFs (Aerts et al., 2018), it is tempting to speculate that the PHE1 binding sites that are present at PEG loci could be shared by a central cell-specific MADS-box TF, and used to initiate PRC2 recruitment to these regions; nevertheless, this hypothesis remains to be tested formally.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited reference.

claim: RC/Helitrons contain PHE1 binding sites.
source: Our work establishes a novel role for RC/Helitrons in the regulation of gene expression by showing that these TEs contain PHE1 binding sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TE overlap analysis.

claim: RC/Helitrons have been domesticated to function as providers of cis-regulatory sequences that facilitate transcription.
source: Our data favor a scenario in which these elements have been domesticated to function as providers of cis-regulatory sequences that facilitate transcription.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed overlap of PHE1 binding sites with RC/Helitrons and the expression patterns of genes flanked by these TEs.

claim: Insertion of RC/Helitrons can contribute to the generation of novel gene promoters that ensure timely expression of nearby genes in the endosperm.
source: Insertion of these elements can contribute to the generation of novel gene promoters that ensure the timely expression of nearby genes in the endosperm, controlled by PHE1 and possibly by other type I MADS-box TFs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed role of RC/Helitrons in carrying PHE1 binding sites.

claim: RC/Helitrons can promote the establishment of epigenetic modifications conducive to imprinting.
source: Given our observation that RC/Helitrons carry PHE DNA-binding motifs, and that these TEs have been previously shown to be associated with PEGs (Hatorangan et al., 2016; Pignatta et al., 2014; Wolff et al., 2011), we propose a dual role for these elements in imprinting. Besides promoting the establishment of epigenetic modifications that are conducive to imprinting (Gehring, 2013; Rodrigues and Zilberman, 2015), they can also contribute to the transcriptional activation of these genes in the endosperm by carrying type I MADS-box TF binding sites.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: RC/Helitrons can contribute to the transcriptional activation of imprinted genes in the endosperm by carrying type I MADS-box TF binding sites.
source: Given our observation that RC/Helitrons carry PHE DNA-binding motifs, and that these TEs have been previously shown to be associated with PEGs (Hatorangan et al., 2016; Pignatta et al., 2014; Wolff et al., 2011), we propose a dual role for these elements in imprinting. Besides promoting the establishment of epigenetic modifications that are conducive to imprinting (Gehring, 2013; Rodrigues and Zilberman, 2015), they can also contribute to the transcriptional activation of these genes in the endosperm by carrying type I MADS-box TF binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed role of RC/Helitrons in carrying PHE1 binding sites and their association with PEGs.

claim: Binding sites for type II MADS-box TFs have been shown to be amplified by TEs.
source: Binding sites for type II MADS-box TFs, as well as for E2F TFs, have been shown to be amplified by TEs (Hénaff et al., 2014; Muiño et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: Binding sites for E2F TFs have been shown to be amplified by TEs.
source: Binding sites for type II MADS-box TFs, as well as for E2F TFs, have been shown to be amplified by TEs (Hénaff et al., 2014; Muiño et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: TE-mediated distribution of TF binding sites throughout flowering plant genomes supports the idea that transposition facilitates the formation of cis-regulatory architectures required to control complex biological processes.
source: These results, together with our study, provide examples of the TE-mediated distribution of TF binding sites throughout flowering plant genomes, adding support to the long-standing idea that transposition facilitates the formation of cis-regulatory architectures that are required to control complex biological processes (Britten and Davidson, 1971; Feschotte, 2008; Hirsch and Springer, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed role of TEs in distributing TF binding sites and established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: TE-mediated distribution of regulatory sequences may have contributed to endosperm evolution by allowing recruitment of crucial developmental genes into a single transcriptional network.
source: We speculate that this process may have contributed to endosperm evolution by allowing the recruitment of crucial developmental genes into a single transcriptional network, regulated by type I MADS-box TFs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed role of RC/Helitrons in distributing PHE1 binding sites.

claim: The diversification of the mammalian placenta has been connected with the dispersal of hundreds of placenta-specific enhancers by endogenous retroviruses.
source: The diversification of the mammalian placenta has been connected with the dispersal of hundreds of placenta-specific enhancers by endogenous retroviruses (Chuong et al., 2013; Dunn-Fletcher et al., 2018), suggesting that TE-mediated distribution of regulatory sequences has been relevant both for the evolution of the endosperm in flowering plants and for the evolution of the mammalian placenta.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited references.

claim: TE-mediated distribution of regulatory sequences has been relevant for the evolution of the endosperm in flowering plants and the mammalian placenta.
source: The diversification of the mammalian placenta has been connected with the dispersal of hundreds of placenta-specific enhancers by endogenous retroviruses (Chuong et al., 2013; Dunn-Fletcher et al., 2018), suggesting that TE-mediated distribution of regulatory sequences has been relevant both for the evolution of the endosperm in flowering plants and for the evolution of the mammalian placenta.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed role of TEs in distributing regulatory sequences in both plants and mammals.
